title: Tighten blocking_guard threshold from 3 to 2 waiting robots
reason: Blocked time is 2404 s, with A alone losing 1352 s and missing 7.8 pickup deadlines, while the eviction guard fires only 2.8 times at k=3. Overstaying past hold_limit only adds a Minor penalty and does not move the robot, so eviction at k=2 is the rule lever that actually clears parked robots from intersections. It should cut A's blocked time and late pickups, raising on_time_deliveries and lowering p95_wait_s without touching the customer promise. A should vote yes. C will likely vote no because it gets Major eviction penalties. B, which both parks and is blocked, is uncertain, so the 2-of-3 quorum may not be met.
assumptions: Eviction physically moves a parked robot off the node, whereas a release-deadline overstay only adds a penalty.
A's late pickups are caused mainly by blocking from robots parked on the road, not by distance or load.
Two robots waiting behind a parked robot happens often enough at 75 s order intervals for k=2 to make a measurable difference.
unknowns: How often the blocking count reaches 2, and therefore how many extra evictions and Major penalties C and B would receive.
Whether evicted robots then travel extra distance and miss their own deadlines.
B's net utility change, since B both parks and is blocked; this decides the vote.

question: Should we adopt block_k 3 → 2 even though companies B and C voted against it, adopt the contract revision pickup_deadline 120s → 150s, or keep the current rules (v1)?
reason: Option 2 is rejected under K1. This is the first SLA revision, so I checked K1.d.f1. p95_wait_s stays at 188, max_wait_s at 385 and unfinished at 0.0, so customers get no faster service. Meanwhile their pickup promise is loosened from 120 s to 150 s. The +0.8 on-time gain (3/5 seeds improved) only relabels late pickups as on time, which is a worse promise with no measured benefit to customers. Option 1 is clearly the best for the KPI: on-time goes from 121.8 to 131.0 (+9.2, 5/5 seeds), late from 10.4 to 1.2, p95_wait_s from 188 to 81.4 and max_wait_s from 385 to 245. However, the company vote is part of the machine judgment, and option 1 lost it (A ○, B ×, C ×). Overriding a two-of-three majority is a serious governance step. It would also impose a heavy loss on C (utility 28.8 to 19.0) and raise road violations from 25.8 to 34.0, which we have not analysed. Departing from the LLM's recommendation of option 1 is deliberate. I prefer to keep v1 for this period and return in period 2 with a version of block_k=2 that the companies can accept, such as a remedy for C or an adjusted design, plus a breakdown of the added road violations. That keeps the measured gain within reach without setting a precedent of overriding the votes.
assumptions: The company vote is a binding part of the machine judgment for rule changes, and overriding it should be reserved for cases with no negotiable alternative.
The gain from block_k=2 will still be available, and can be re-proposed in a modified form, next period.
Keeping v1 for one more period causes no customer harm beyond the current baseline (late 10.4, p95_wait_s 188).
unknowns: Why B and C voted against block_k=2, and what remedy or modified threshold would change their votes.
Which road violations increase under block_k=2 and how severe they are.
Demand in period 2, and whether option 1's gain holds under different load.
How customers perceive the current 120 s pickup promise compared with 150 s.

title: Targeted C remedy for measurement: hold_limit 60s → 70s
reason: C's whole utility gap (8.4 vs 27-29) comes from 21.4 release-deadline overstays at the 60 s hold_limit. A 70 s limit targets exactly that behaviour without undoing the lambda 1 enforcement adopted in D5. On-time cannot rise by more than 0.2 here, so the change will fail the min_improvement gate. It is offered to measure C's relief against any rise in p95/max wait and blocked_s in a quiet period. D4 rejected this change in a busy period because every customer measure worsened. What differs now is the D5 request for a C remedy, the higher lambda baseline and the quiet demand. Since the rule also applies in busy periods, the D4 harm remains a reason to reject it. Expected vote: C yes; A and B probably yes only if their on-time counts stay at the ceiling.
assumptions: C's 22.6 sanction points come almost entirely from the 21.4 release overstays at 60 s, as the arithmetic (21.4×1 + 0.4×3) suggests.
Many of C's road holds end between 60 s and 70 s, so a 10 s longer limit removes a meaningful share of them.
unknowns: How C's hold durations are distributed, i.e. how many overstays fall between 60 and 70 s.
Whether the longer holds raise blocking for A and B enough to cost them deliveries even in a quiet period.
Whether the D4 busy-period harm would recur under lambda 1 instead of 0.5.

question: Should the C-specific remedy hold_limit 60s → 70s be adopted, even though it fails the 1.0 minimum-improvement gate and raises customer wait times, or should the rules stay at v2?

why.reason: LLM: This is the C-specific remedy the human requested in D5. It cannot pass the 1.0 min_improvement gate because on-time is at the ceiling (0.2 headroom). In D4 the same change was rejected in a busy period for worsening every customer measure. The human must weigh C's relief against that earlier customer harm and decide whether a measurement-only result is useful.

options.summary: Adopt hold_limit 60s → 70s. On-time 87.2 → 87.4 (+0.2, 1/5 seeds improved), late 0.2 → 0.0, lowest on-time rate 0.99 → 1.00, unfinished stays 0.0. Customer waits worsen: p95_wait_s 79.8 → 84.2 and max_wait_s 113 → 127. Blocked s rises 521 → 589, while road violations fall 21.8 → 20.6. Utility A/B/C goes from 27.4 / 28.8 / 8.4 to 27.6 / 28.8 / 8.8. Votes are unanimous (A ○, B ○, C ○), but the change misses the min_improvement gate, so adopting it needs your explicit decision.
options.affected: C gains a little (8.4 → 8.8) and A gains slightly (27.4 → 27.6); B is unchanged. Customers lose on waiting time: the typical slow wait (p95) is about 4.4 s longer and the worst case 14 s longer, in exchange for roughly 0.2 fewer late deliveries per run. Other road users face more blocking (589 vs 521 blocked s).

options.summary: Stay at v2 (sanction_lambda 1, hold_limit 60s). On-time 87.2, late 0.2, p95_wait_s 79.8, max_wait_s 113, unfinished 0.0, blocked s 521, road violations 21.8, utility A/B/C 27.4 / 28.8 / 8.4. The D5 request for a C remedy stays open.
options.affected: Customers keep the shorter p95 and worst-case waits. C stays the lowest-utility company at 8.4 with no remedy. A and B are essentially unaffected. All three companies would have accepted option 1, so keeping v2 goes against a unanimous preference.

reason: Under K1, any rise in p95_wait_s or max_wait_s is customer worsening that needs a measured justification. Option 1 raises p95_wait_s 79.8 → 84.2 and max_wait_s 113 → 127. Its only customer gain is +0.2 on-time with 1/5 seeds improved, which is within noise and below the gate. C's relief is small (8.4 → 8.8) and does not address C's structural position. The same change worsened every customer measure in the busy D4 period, so adopting it risks larger harm when demand rises. The unanimous vote does not change this: customers do not vote, and in D3 and D4 a passing vote did not oblige adoption when customer measures worsened. A better C remedy should be sought, for example a change to how sanctions are distributed or to C's hold behaviour that does not lengthen customer waits.
assumptions: The 5-seed measurement represents the next period's demand, which may be busier as in D4.
C's low utility comes mainly from sanctions on overstays under sanction_lambda 1, so a hold-limit change only partly addresses it.
A, B and C would accept continuing at v2 without strong objection.
unknowns: Whether next period's demand will be busy, as in D4, where this change worsened every customer measure.
Why C's utility is so low under v2: the breakdown of C's sanctions, holds and deliveries has not been measured.
How customers perceive a roughly 14 s longer worst-case wait compared with 0.2 fewer late deliveries.
Each company's behaviour policy, and whether C would change its overstay behaviour under a different remedy.
Whether you will count a measurement-only result as progress on D5.f1, or require an adopted remedy.
The per-company breakdown of road violations and blocked seconds under option 1.

question: Should the C-specific remedy hold_limit 60s → 70s be adopted, even though it fails the 1.0 minimum-improvement gate and raises customer wait times, or should the rules stay at v2?
reason:
I stay at v2 (sanction_lambda 1, hold_limit 60s) and follow the LLM's recommendation. Under K1, any rise in p95_wait_s or max_wait_s is customer worsening that needs a measured justification. Option 1 does not provide one.

The customer cost is measured:
- p95_wait_s rises from 79.8 to 84.2;
- max_wait_s rises from 113 to 127;
- blocked s rises from 521 to 589.

The customer gain is not measured with any confidence. On-time rises only from 87.2 to 87.4 (+0.2), with 1/5 seeds improved. Late falls from 0.2 to 0.0. This is within noise and below the 1.0 min_improvement gate.

In D4 the same change worsened every customer measure in a busy period, so adopting it risks larger harm when demand rises. C's relief is small (8.4 to 8.8) and does not address why C's utility is low.

Departing from the unanimous vote (A ○, B ○, C ○) is deliberate. Customers do not vote. As in D3 and D4, a passing vote does not oblige adoption when customer waits worsen without a measured gain to justify it.

This measurement does not count as the C remedy I asked for in D5. D5.f2 also required an analysis of which C behaviours incur sanctions, and C's view; neither was provided. D5.f2 stays open.
assumptions: The period-6 measurements are representative of quiet periods under v2.
The +0.2 on-time gain is noise, given only 1/5 seeds improved.
C's low utility mainly comes from overstay sanctions under lambda 1, as stated in D5.
unknowns: The breakdown of C's sanctions, holds and deliveries under v2.
Whether the next period will be busy.
Whether a scoped sanction adjustment could raise C's utility without lengthening customer waits.
C's own view on which remedy it would accept.
